content: The file Cslib.Languages.LambdaCalculus.LocallyNameless.Fsub.Safety always takes a long time to compile on my machine. All other files combined seem to take a comparable amount of time. Is there something we can do performance-optimize this file?

More generally the Lakeprof Report shows that the System F modules form our critical path. These performance issues are due to the usage of grind annotations that are too wide. You can see some culprits in CslibTests/GrindLint.lean. This is on my todo list, but PRs making some initial tradeoffs between performance and compact proofs are welcome! I had started looking at this a bit in CSLib#283 for reference. Some of the existing rules could also maybe be made more performant by using the constraint feature of grind_pattern, which would be preferable to removing annotations completely.
(also we should discuss having a cache at some point, but that shouldn't mean we avoid fixing this performance)
Can you achieve the effect of this inlining by forcing grind only?

The Mathlib style guide does not have an entry on grind yet, but my intuition is that we should treat it similarly to simp in terms of considering terminal squeezing undesirable. I'd much rather fix or inline the annotations than have them polluting a scope with over instantiation that you always have to ignore with a grind only.
The difficulty is, it is much harder to find grind lemmas. Inlining everything for grind also defeats half the benefits of a powerful tactic.

Let me clarify my preferred order of fixes:

  • keeping an annotation, but limiting its instantiation with grind_pattern or a more specific rule
  • removing the annotation and inlining, especially when it is not used often
  • using grind only, preferably limited to situations where a proof breaks across toolchains or very extreme performance implications
  • removing the grind usage entirely

I am not advocating for "inlining everything". We are talking about a pretty specific set of theorems, and just like with simp it is sometimes desirable to only manually include a theorem for use with grind.
My guess is that some things have been overzealously tagged with grind; for instance, tagging every definition with grind is basically saying "I can't be bothered to write lemmas about this"

Yes, and this was some of the first uses of grind I experimented with, I think "overzealous" is accurate. The first step should probably be me stepping through everything by hand and thinking about what really should be tagged or not.
And as the one who wrote and now maintains it, I'll take primary ownership of untangling this. There is also some similar work I am doing for LTS.

Eric Wieser said:

My guess is that some things have been overzealously tagged with grind; for instance, tagging every definition with grind is basically saying "I can't be bothered to write lemmas about this"

This sounds like the sort of thing where grind could create an auxiliary file and add the lemmas and re use it the next time. I know I am reinventing cache here, but I mean something like a cache of lemmas specific to grind that is only regenerated when the declaration tagged with grind is changed.
